description: We are a student team from SAMA 5 Middle School, passionate about aerospace, space exploration, science, and technology. We are excited to learn, collaborate, experiment, and turn creative ideas into real solutions.
summary: Silent Sentinels is an interactive, story-driven web experience that introduces school-age learners to the NASA hardware left on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space. Instead of presenting mission archives as technical catalogues, the project treats each dormant rover, lander, descent stage, instrument, and probe as a "silent sentinel"—a witness that holds the record of a mission and a discovery. The experience has three layers: an interactive map for breadth, mission-file story cards for depth, and a guided learning path for sequence. Each card follows a six-part narrative template—hook, identity, mission, discovery, fate, and a clearly labeled first-person retelling based on real mission data—with specifications moved into a collapsible drawer. Accuracy is protected by a source hierarchy, a one-page fact sheet per artifact, a two-person fact-checking rule, a "what we simplified" transparency note, and a verified-source badge linked to NASA and JPL pages. Accessibility is built in from the start: alt text, transcripts, keyboard navigation, and a text-list alternative to the map. The project addresses the challenge by turning complex historical and scientific data into an engaging narrative that inspires young learners and helps them understand how engineering enables scientific discovery.
details:
What it does and how it works. Silent Sentinels is a static, data-driven web experience with three connected layers. Layer 1 is an interactive map of the Moon, Mars, and deep space with clickable markers for each artifact and a text-list alternative. Layer 2 is a mission-file story card for each artifact, following a six-part template: hook, identity, mission, discovery, fate, and "in its own words." Layer 3 is a guided learning path with a timeline, comic panels, audio clips with transcripts, prediction and comparison questions, and reflection prompts. Content is stored as JSON, one object per artifact, and rendered by a single template, so non-developers can author stories without touching code.

Benefits. The project solves an access problem, not an information problem. Mission archives are abundant but organized for specialists; learners meet launch dates and instrument lists before finding a reason to care. Silent Sentinels inverts that order: the story comes first, and technical detail lives in a collapsible drawer that opens only on request. The result is content that a young learner can follow, trust, and remember, and that a teacher can use with confidence.

Intended impact. Impact is defined at three levels: knowledge (the learner can name an artifact, describe where it is, and explain one discovery), understanding (the learner sees how engineering enables science), and inspiration (the learner forms a personal connection to a machine that will never come home). Longer-term impact includes scientific and media literacy—the labeled retellings and transparency notes teach the difference between dramatization and fabrication—and broader representation of the people behind space exploration.

Tools, languages, and software. HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the front end; SVG or a lightweight map library for the map; JSON for content; native HTML audio for narration; static hosting for deployment. The design is mobile-first and tested on phone, tablet, and laptop, with keyboard-only and screen-reader checks against a WCAG 2.1 AA baseline.

Creativity. Three choices make the project distinctive. First, the "silent sentinel" framing treats dormant hardware as witnesses rather than failures. Second, the first-person narrative is paired with explicit honesty framing—every retelling is labeled as based on real mission data—so imagination and accuracy coexist. Third, the three-layer architecture lets one body of content serve exploration, depth, and guided learning without duplicating authoring work.

Factors considered. Scope discipline (eight artifacts, four categories, a defined minimum viable product); scientific accuracy (source hierarchy, one-page fact sheets, a two-person fact-checking rule, verified-source badges, "what we simplified" notes); accessibility (alt text, transcripts, captions, keyboard navigation, contrast, text alternative to the map, mobile-first design); privacy for minors (no accounts, no data collection, no trackers); and sustainability (static stack, open JSON schema, translation-ready text fields).
